title: Shams arrives
hookLine: in 1244 a wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, meets Rumi, and his life turns (the accounts are part history, part legend)

cards: Some people walk into your life and nothing is the same afterward. A teacher who saw something in you. A stranger on a train.
The person you married. You can usually name the day. For Rumi, it came in the autumn of 1244.
He was about thirty-seven, settled, respected, sure of his path. Into Konya came an older man, perhaps in his sixties, a wandering dervish in a rough cloak, from the city of Tabriz.
He had no school, no post and no patience for either. His name was Shams, which means sun.

teach.b: First, the honest part. Much of what's told about this meeting comes from biographies written decades later by devoted followers, and they read partly as history and partly as legend. So hold the stories lightly.
In one, Rumi is riding through the market with his students. Shams grabs his bridle and asks a question.
Who was greater, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, or the Sufi Bayazid, who said startling things about his own closeness to God? Rumi answers: the Prophet.
Bayazid's thirst was quenched by one sip; the Prophet's thirst was endless, and he kept asking for more. In some tellings Rumi faints.
In another story, Shams throws the scholar's books into water, then pulls them out dry. Nobody can prove any of it. What is solid is what happened next.
The two men shut themselves away for weeks, maybe months, talking, praying, fasting. Rumi stopped teaching. His students were furious and jealous: who was this beggar who had taken their master?
Shams's own voice survives, too, because his sayings were written down in a book called the Maqalat, the Discourses.
He comes across as blunt, funny and fierce, impatient with people who knew about God from books but had never tasted anything.
The respected scholar had met someone who asked whether he knew what he knew. And he answered by changing his life.

how: The meeting of Rumi and Shams is told in the old biographies by Sipahsalar and Aflaki, which blend history and legend, and readers of Rumi still retell it as the turning point of his life.

o: the day Rumi's family first reached Konya from the east

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

Shams was a young student of Rumi's

games.q: you're Rumi, riding through the market. a stranger grabs your bridle and asks who was greater, the Prophet or Bayazid. what do you say?
o: the Prophet: his thirst for God was endless.
Bayazid: he spoke of great closeness to God.
games.why: in the story Rumi answers: the Prophet. Bayazid was satisfied by one sip; the Prophet kept asking for more. it's a legend, but it's the one the old biographies tell.

practice: Let one person come to mind whose arrival turned something, gently or roughly, long ago or last year. Where were you, what did they say or just do, and what changed afterward?
If you can, feel a little gratitude, even if it was hard, and if they're still alive, notice whether they know what they did.

wordCard.voice: Shams arrives. In 1244 a wandering dervish from Tabriz meets the scholar of Konya, and Rumi's life turns. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: the sun. Shams al-Din, the sun of the faith, from Tabriz.

carryVoice: Your line: someone arrives. One hundred sixty days in, and the story has taken a turn.
